question: What is the difference between composition and inheritance?
title: Composition vs Inheritance — has-a vs is-a
direct_answer: **Inheritance** is an **is-a** relationship — Dog extends Animal means Dog IS-A Animal. It inherits all methods and state. **Composition** is a **has-a** relationship — Car has-a Engine, implemented by holding a field of type Engine. Inheritance is static (set at compile time), composition is dynamic (the held object can be swapped at runtime).

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking inheritance is always better because it reuses code — composition is usually safer and more flexible
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Lead with the GoF principle: favor composition over inheritance

sections.title: Composition vs Inheritance
sections.content:
| Aspect | Inheritance | Composition |
|--------|-------------|-------------|
| Relationship | is-a | has-a |
| Coupling | Tight (subclass knows parent internals) | Loose (holds reference to interface) |
| Flexibility | Static — set at compile time | Dynamic — can swap at runtime |
| Testing | Harder — parent state affects tests | Easier — inject mock collaborator |
| Reuse | Inherited methods | Delegated to held object |

sections.title: How to say this in an interview
sections.content: Inheritance is the is-a relationship — Dog extends Animal says a Dog is an Animal and inherits everything. Composition is the has-a relationship — Car has an Engine, meaning Car holds a reference to an Engine object and delegates engine-related behavior to it. The key difference is flexibility: inheritance is locked in at compile time, whereas composition lets me swap the held object at runtime. That is why the GoF book says: favor composition over inheritance.

direct_answer: Composition is preferred because it is **more flexible** (swap collaborators at runtime), **less coupled** (depends on interface, not parent implementation), and **easier to test** (inject mocks). sections.title: Problems with inheritance
sections.content: 1. Fragile base class: changing a method in the parent can break subclasses that relied on the old behavior. 2. Tight coupling: subclasses depend on parent implementation details — a white-box relationship. 3. Limited flexibility: Java only allows single inheritance, so using inheritance for one thing blocks you from inheriting something else. 4. Hard to test: you cannot easily replace the parent's behavior in a subclass test. Composition avoids all of these.

sections.title: How to say this in an interview
sections.content: Composition is preferred because inheritance creates tight coupling between a subclass and its parent. If the parent changes an internal method, all subclasses can break — this is called the fragile base class problem. Also, Java only allows single inheritance, so using it up on one relationship limits your options. Composition is more flexible: I hold a reference to an interface, I can swap the implementation, and in tests I can inject a mock. The GoF book summed it up: favor composition over inheritance.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 Spring Boot app applying SOLID principles
speakable_v2.hook: The fragile base class problem is when a small parent refactor silently breaks a subclass with no compiler warning.

beats.content: When a subclass overrides a method and the parent's other methods internally call that method, the subclass behavior depends on that internal chain. If the parent refactors to stop using that internal call, the subclass behavior changes silently. No compile error, just wrong results.

The LoggingCounter example shows it clearly. LoggingCounter overrides add() to count calls. Counter's addAll() calls add() internally, so three items means three add() calls. If Counter later refactors addAll() to not call add(), LoggingCounter's count becomes zero. The subclass depended on a private implementation detail.

sharp edge: this problem doesn't exist with composition because you hold a reference to an interface, not an implementation. You delegate to the held object's public contract only. No dependency on internal call chains.

speakable_v2.cap: Fragile base class: subclasses depending on parent internals break silently when the parent refactors. Composition avoids this by only depending on public contracts.

question: What is the fragile base class problem?
title: Fragile base class problem in Java inheritance
direct_answer: The **fragile base class problem** occurs when a change to a parent class breaks one or more subclasses, even though the parent change seemed correct and harmless. Because subclasses depend on the parent's internal behavior, any change to the parent — even small refactors — can have unexpected effects on inherited or overriding subclass code.

question: When is inheritance the right choice over composition?
title: When to use inheritance — valid use cases
direct_answer: Inheritance is appropriate when: (1) there is a **true is-a relationship** where the subclass truly is a specialized version of the parent, (2) the subclass needs most of the parent's behavior and differs only in specifics, (3) you want to take advantage of **polymorphism** to treat subclasses uniformly. The test: is the subclass a kind of the parent, or does it just use some of its behavior?

sections.title: Good use cases for inheritance
sections.content: Use inheritance when: 1) Cat extends Animal — Cat truly is an Animal with all its behaviors. 2) You use the Template Method pattern — parent defines structure, subclass fills in steps. 3) You need runtime polymorphism — treat List<Animal> with both Cat and Dog objects. 4) The subclass uses most of the parent and only overrides 1-2 methods. Avoid inheritance when: you want to reuse just 1-2 methods — that is the wrong reason, use composition.

sections.title: How to say this in an interview
sections.content: Inheritance is the right choice when there is a genuine is-a relationship where the subclass is truly a specialized kind of the parent. If Cat extends Animal makes sense because a cat is an animal with all the behaviors of one, that is good inheritance. Inheritance is also the right choice for the Template Method pattern where the parent defines a process and subclasses fill in specific steps. The wrong reason to use inheritance is just to reuse a couple of methods — that is what composition is for.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 Spring Boot app applying SOLID principles
speakable_v2.hook: The Decorator pattern is the textbook example of composition over inheritance, and Java IO uses it everywhere.

beats.content: Instead of creating MilkCoffee, SugarCoffee, and MilkSugarCoffee as separate subclasses, the Decorator pattern creates a MilkDecorator that wraps any Coffee object. It implements Coffee itself, holds a Coffee reference, and adds milk behavior while delegating everything else to the wrapped object.

The power is runtime composition. You can combine decorators in any order: new MilkDecorator(new SugarDecorator(new SimpleCoffee())). With inheritance you'd need a separate class for every combination. With decoration you compose freely.

non-obvious: Java IO uses this pattern throughout. BufferedReader wraps FileReader. GZIPInputStream wraps FileInputStream. Every wrapper is a decorator that adds behavior through composition. If Java had used inheritance instead, the class hierarchy would be enormous. Knowing this real-world example shows you've actually used composition in production code.

speakable_v2.cap: Decorator uses composition to combine behaviors at runtime. Much more flexible than a class per combination using inheritance.

question: How does the Decorator pattern use composition instead of inheritance?
title: Decorator pattern — composition to extend behavior at runtime
direct_answer: The **Decorator pattern** uses **composition** to add behavior to an object without subclassing. A decorator wraps the original object (holds it as a field implementing the same interface) and adds behavior before or after delegating to the original. This allows combining features at runtime without a class explosion from inheritance.
